Background The number of commercial coal, gas, and nuclear projects built over the past 100 years number in the thousands. As such, there is a large database, available to a wide range of commercial engineering contractors, on proven designs. In essence, unsuccessful designs have, through generations of iterations, been identified, and then deleted from possible consideration. In contrast, the number of commercial parabolic trough projects using nitrate salt for the thermal storage media is perhaps 60. Further, the number of commercial central receiver projects using nitrate salt as the working fluid is on the order of 20, including estimates for China. As such, commercial solar technologies have not progressed through the same number of design iterations as fossil and nuclear technologies. This results in 1) the persistence of problems normally seen with first-of-a-kind designs, and 2) a range of problems, yet unresolved, that preclude solar projects from reaching the availabilities required for market acceptance (92+ percent). The problem is compounded by levelized energy prices for solar projects which are often higher than energy prices for fossil projects. This can lead solar project developers to bid projects with low energy prices to attract the capital investment, but the prices are too low to fully reflect the performance risks inherent in an technology that is undergoing iteration. On a related point, there are likely a range of performance requirements that a plant must satisfy to meet a competitive energy price, but the requirements impose a floor on the design features and the capital cost. One feature is the tube-to-tubesheet connection in a steam generator heat exchanger. As an example, the heat exchanger must tolerate 30,000 daily startup and shutdown cycles, at a temperature change rate of 12 °C/min, if the plant is to meet its annual performance target. Candidate tube-to- tubesheet connections include 1) rolled and strength welded, 2) internal bore welded, and 3) welded header/coil. Option 1 is the least expensive, but it can accommodate rates of temperature change of only 8 to 10 °C/min. Options 2 and 3 incur a cost premium of perhaps 30 percent over Option 1, but both can satisfy the transient requirements. As such, the project must select either Option 2 or Option 3, and reflect the higher capital cost in the energy sales price in the Power Purchase Agreement. If a project is to be successful, it cannot, as has been tried in other commercial projects, bid the low-cost steam generator option and then, through magical thinking, expect to match the projections in the performance model. The Design Basis Document / Owner’s Technical Specification is a first step in the iteration process.
